name: Café Noir
lede: Café Noir is a dark, slightly reddish brown named for black coffee, and the ISCC-NBS dictionary files it as a dark yellowish brown.

sections.title: From a 1928 plate to a 1955 dictionary
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary of color dates the name to 1928, at plate 8, column H, chip 12, hex #4B3621 [1]. The ISCC-NBS committee cited the same swatch in 1955, in block 81 among the "dark yellowish brown" names, 3.1 units from that block's center [1]. The Munsell renotation is 9.5YR 2.4/2.9, a dark, fairly low-chroma brown [1]. Wikipedia's color-name list also cites the ISCC-NBS entry [1].

The nearest library names are [[ivory-brown]], about three units away, and [[falcon]], a touch darker and redder, at 4.8 units [1]. The French name itself is not explained beyond the obvious translation, "black coffee"; who coined the color name is undocumented here [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: A color within six units of Café Noir covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 8,782 of 23,781 paintings, about 37 per cent, as photographed [2]. That is an unusually wide net for a single named brown: it is one of the most common shadow and underpainting tones in the archive, not a rare named hue [2]. It peaks in the 1630s, in 332 of 833 paintings, and Dutch painters dominate the top of the list: Otto van Veen, Nicolaes Maes and Jan Both each carry it in more than four out of five of their paintings, roughly twice the archive's overall rate [2]. Its earliest appearance is a Buddhist triad dated to around 900 [2]. These are photographs of varnished paintings, read as screen colors [2].
